entries.title: Your Architecture Was Built to Run, Not to Explain Itself
entries.description: Enterprise architectures were designed to process transactions, not to supply the context intelligence needs. Classic AI finds the anomaly, GenAI explains it, and only a reworked architecture can act on it.
entries.text: Intelligence can find the anomaly and explain it. Only a reworked architecture can act on it. I was reading a HackerNoon piece on monitoring event-driven architectures this week, and one line stayed with me: successfully publishing an event does not mean the business process completed successfully. That sentence describes far more than event-driven systems. It describes how most enterprise architecture has been designed for decades. We built systems to run. We never built them to explain themselves. The broker is healthy. The business is not. The article lays out a familiar problem. In a point-to-point design, failures surface on their own through connection errors and missing acknowledgments. In an event-driven design, the broker queues messages when a consumer disconnects. Nothing is lost, so the broker looks healthy, even when processing has quietly stopped. The author gives two failure modes worth thinking about. A stop-sell event fans out to regional channel servers, and not all of them receive or process it. A consumer instance crashes but keeps receiving messages without acknowledging them, so messages pile up and compute is wasted. The recommended answer is a sensible combination: APM tools evaluating multiple conditions together, application-level publish and consume rates, and heartbeat events that validate the path end to end. All of it is good engineering. And all of it is static. Alert when a critical queue has more than five spooled messages and no bound client, three times in ten minutes. Investigate when throughput drops, and accept the false positives. These are human guesses encoded as thresholds. The real gap is not detection. It is that none of these signals can tell you whether a business outcome is at risk, why, or what to do about it. Numbers tell you what. Text tells you why. Most of my work before generative AI was on metric streams and time series. Incident avoidance, which I started building about ten years ago, began by extracting business KPIs from historical data, setting up time-series observation on them, and then layering infrastructure metric streams underneath. Anomaly detection on numbers is powerful. It tells you something changed and when. What it cannot tell you is what that change means. That is where our journey moved from classic AI to generative AI. We used GenAI to read through textual data, including logs, tickets and user complaints, and build dispositions for decisions and causation. A user complaint confirms the anomaly. When a user says order processing is slow, and a synthetic transaction monitor shows order processing time climbing at the same moment, you have two independent signals pointing at the same business impact. The text reinforces the numbers. Text points toward causation. Logs and ticket history carry the context that metrics strip away: which step, which dependency, which change, which pattern has been seen before. Together, they earn the right to act. Correlation alone should never trigger an automated action on infrastructure or applications. Correlation reinforced by text, and validated against historical patterns, can. The simplest way I can put it: classic AI finds the anomaly, GenAI explains it, and the architecture has to be able to act on it. That last part is where most enterprises are stuck. Bolting intelligence onto mute systems Whether the architecture is event-driven, request-response, batch or a mainframe at the core, the pattern is the same. Every one of these can be reinforced with intelligence today. But most were never designed to take part in it. Logs were written for a developer debugging at 2 a.m., not for correlation with business entities. Telemetry describes components, not outcomes. And there is rarely a safe, governed way for an intelligent system to do anything other than raise an alert. So enterprises bolt AI on top. They add an AIOps layer, an observability platform, an agent. The intelligence can see more, but it is still working with systems that cannot explain themselves and cannot accept corrective action. That caps the value, no matter how good the model is. This is the same mistake we make with process. Automating a broken process just gives you a faster broken process. That is why I argue for eliminating first, then automating, then seeking human assist. Architecture deserves the same treatment. Before you layer intelligence on top, rework the architecture so it can take part in its own intelligence. What the rework looks like This is not a rip-and-replace argument. It is a design argument. Three changes matter most. Emit meaning, not just telemetry. Systems should carry business context in what they emit: the order, the claim, the customer, the process step. Events should carry their expected outcome and the time within which it should happen. Consumers should confirm that the business outcome happened, not just that a message arrived. That alone closes the gap the HackerNoon piece describes: the stop-sell event was published, but did every region actually stop selling? Expose safe ways to act. Intelligence that cannot act stops at a notification to email or Teams. Applications and infrastructure need governed action points: scale, divert, restart, replay, roll back. In my own work, safe diversion became a core action, meaning an alternate path known to take the load, the way full self-driving moves over instead of braking hard. The objective is near-zero MTTR with no business disruption, not a faster page to an on-call engineer. That requires the diversion paths, idempotent replay and limits on how much a single action can affect to be designed in, not discovered during an incident. Close the feedback loop. Every action and its outcome should flow back into historical intelligence. What was detected, what the text said, what action was taken, and whether the business outcome recovered. This is how the system learns what fixed what, and how humans stay in the loop to correct it, until the track record earns more autonomy. APM doesn’t go away. Its job changes. None of this makes APM tools, broker statistics or heartbeats obsolete. They cover real gaps, and they should stay. What changes is their role. Today they mostly end in dashboards and alerts for a human to interpret. In an intelligence-ready architecture, they become inputs: numeric signals fused with textual signals, evaluated against historical patterns of good and bad behavior, feeding decisions that the architecture is built to carry out. The foundation under all of it is the one I keep coming back to: discovery and dependency mapping attached to past behaviors. Loose coupling is good design, but it hides who depends on whom. The more loosely coupled the architecture, the more that map matters, because the dependencies are no longer visible in the code. The question for architects Every architecture review I have seen asks whether the system will scale, whether it is secure, and whether it can be monitored. I would add one more question: can this system explain itself, and can it accept corrective action? If the answer is no, the intelligence you buy will see the problem, describe it beautifully, and then wait for a human, just like the threshold alert it replaced. Architectures that have run enterprises for decades are due for this kind of renewal. Not because the technology is legacy, but because they were built to run, and the next decade will ask them to explain themselves and act. This article is part of the Enterprise Intelligence series on building intelligence that drives peak business performance.

entries.title: Intelligence Has to Earn the Name
entries.description: Intelligence implies purpose — solving a problem humans can’t solve in time, at consistent quality, or at scale. From business intelligence to AI coding, we keep attaching the word to tools that never stated the problem.
entries.text: Intelligence implies purpose — solving a problem humans can’t solve in time, at consistent quality, or at scale. From business intelligence to AI coding, we keep attaching the word to tools that never stated the problem. I have never understood why a whole category of software was called business intelligence. Most of what carried that label was a query tool with good charts. You asked a question, it returned an answer. It never knew why you asked. It didn’t know which outcome the business was trying to move, whether the number on the dashboard was good or bad, or what should happen next. A human did all of that. The intelligence was in the analyst, not the tool. That isn’t a knock on what those tools did. Giving people access to data mattered. But the name promised something the tools never delivered, and I think we’re repeating that mistake with AI. What the word should mean Intelligence implies purpose. It’s in the word. Being intelligent means solving a problem intelligently : reaching a better outcome than you would have otherwise. For enterprise systems, I’d say intelligence earns the name when it does three things: It serves a stated purpose. There is a business outcome it is accountable for, such as claims cycle time, order-to-delivery or onboarding speed, and it is measured against that outcome, not against its own activity. It does what humans can’t do well enough. That means work a person can’t do in the time available, can’t do with consistent quality, or can’t do at the scale the business needs. It leads to a decision or an action. It doesn’t just return what was asked. It reaches a disposition and moves the outcome. Take any one of these away and you have a faster tool, not an intelligent one. The same trap, new clothes Communications of the ACM published a piece this week on scaling AI-enabled coding. It cites CircleCI’s 2026 State of Software Delivery: more code was being written, yet the rate of finished, released work fell . AI-generated code failed more often and took longer to fix. One line in the piece stands out: “Writing code was never really the bottleneck.” Run AI coding through the test above. Does it serve a stated purpose? Mostly it has been measured on code generated and developer velocity, which describe activity, not outcomes. Does it do what humans can’t? It types faster, but typing was never the constraint. Does it move the outcome? The delivery data says not yet. This is business intelligence all over again. A capability arrived, the word “intelligent” got attached, and the problem was never stated. AI coding came in the way full self-driving did: exciting and new, but not something anyone was asking for. An electric vehicle answered a plain need, which was lower fuel cost. Technology push isn’t wrong in itself, but at some point the need has to be named. The article also introduces Margaret-Anne Storey’s idea of intent debt : the missing record of goals, constraints and rationale, so nobody knows what a system is actually for. That’s the cost of intelligence without purpose, and it doesn’t start in the codebase. It starts when nobody writes down which business outcome the work is meant to serve. How we started: purpose first When I was asked to build a platform for managed services that could be positioned and sold differently, the brief didn’t mention a model. It came down to a question: what would make this different? The answer was intelligence built from historical operational data. As we worked through years of that data, a pattern stood out: operations quietly failing a promise. Over time I came to name that promise peak business performance . That became the purpose, and elimination became the way to deliver it. Eliminate the work that shouldn’t exist, automate what can’t be eliminated, and bring in human assist where judgment is needed. Then came the “humans can’t do this well enough” test. Many steps in our data pipeline were extremely difficult or slow for engineers to do at scale, and two engineers looking at the same history would reach different conclusions. That’s what justified the models. We started with classic AI and moved to generative AI as the work required it. The models were chosen because a stated purpose needed them. It didn’t work the other way around. The question to ask before calling anything intelligent Before an enterprise calls its next investment “intelligent,” whether it’s an agent, a copilot, an AI coding platform or a dashboard, it should be able to answer three questions in one sentence each: 1. Which business outcome is this accountable for? 2. What can it do that our people can’t do in time, consistently, or at scale? 3. What decision or action does it take, and what did it eliminate? If those answers are missing, it may still be a useful tool. It just hasn’t earned the name. This article is part of the Enterprise Intelligence series on building intelligence that drives peak business performance.

entries.title: Incident Avoidance Has an ROI Problem, Not a Technology Problem
entries.description: Microsoft’s November 12 outage wasn’t caused by legacy technology. It was caused by an operating model that detects and recovers instead of avoiding, and by an ROI model that can’t see an incident that never happened.
entries.text: Microsoft’s November 12 outage wasn’t caused by legacy technology. It was caused by an operating model that detects and recovers instead of avoiding, and by an ROI model that can’t see an incident that never happened. A recent headline grouped Chase, Microsoft and United together as companies facing crippling outages, and pointed at the usual suspect: legacy, outdated technology. It’s a convenient story. It’s also wrong. Look at each of them. Microsoft. On November 12, Microsoft 365, among the most modern, most instrumented services on the planet, was out for close to a day. Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot were disrupted worldwide. Banks, government offices and trading desks fell back to phones. Some fell back to fax. And this isn’t the first time this year. In July, a network maintenance change in Azure’s West US region rippled into Microsoft 365 as well. None of it was legacy. United. United’s biggest disruption this year was a planned four-and-a-half-hour full system shutdown to move decades-old mainframe systems onto a new cloud architecture. The outage came from the modernization itself, not from the mainframes. Chase. JPMorgan Chase has been detecting fraud in real time across millions of transactions for well over a decade. It owns patents in the space and has invested heavily in the platforms behind it. That is streaming data, anomaly detection and pattern intelligence at scale. The capability exists inside the same company. It just isn’t pointed at its own infrastructure and applications the same way. And plenty of enterprises still run mainframes with little or no issues. The difference was never the age of the technology. It’s architecture, design, and intent. What the preliminary report actually says Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report is out, with the final review due November 20. It describes three factors that lined up. A latent defect. A fix made specifically for the Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers began deploying in July. It introduced lock contention in an internal Windows process that, under certain loads, exhausted CPU and memory. It ran worldwide for more than three months without impact. A load surge. About 15 hours before the outage, Teams traffic failed over from an alternative gateway onto the primary gateway, the same one that fronts Exchange Online. Reduced capacity. Nearly 14% of gateway capacity was already offline from an unrelated issue the day before. On its own, the report says, that had no impact because of spare headroom. Together, they cascaded. At the lowest point, more than 80% of gateway servers were unresponsive. The report also notes that testing had leaned toward lower-core machines, while the contention gets worse on newer, higher-core hardware. And the normal bulkheads between partitions didn’t stop the failure from spreading. Read that list again. Not one of those three conditions was unknown. A recent change on a critical path. A failover onto that path. Capacity already reduced. Each was visible. What was missing was something that evaluated them together. Machines don’t fail suddenly There is a belief in IT operations that outages are sudden, that change-induced failures are unpredictable, that some incidents simply can’t be seen coming. I don’t accept that. A machine, whether it’s a router, a server or an application, doesn’t suddenly produce a fault. It shows a pattern first. Old routers show rising error counts and retransmits long before they fail. And a change-induced incident should simply not happen today. Every enterprise has change advisory boards, approval workflows, test environments, staged rollouts. Yet a change that passed all of that sat in production for three months and then took down a global service. When that happens, the approvals and the testing weren’t informed by anything. Nobody asked what similar changes did before, which services they touched, under what load and capacity they failed, and how far the damage spread. That’s not an unpredictable change. That’s a change approval process without intelligence behind it. Wherever there is a machine, there is a known problem behavior pattern, exactly or close, waiting to be captured. The work is to break the problem into smaller ones: each device class, each change type, each service path, each with its own history. Treated as one giant problem, infrastructure monitoring looks unbounded. Broken down, every piece becomes as tractable as fraud detection. The car doesn’t diagnose the rock Think about how autonomous driving handles this. A car is closing in fast. The system doesn’t stop to work out why there’s traffic, or what the root cause of the other driver’s speed might be. It has already modeled the scenario. It acts on safety first, and analysis comes later. It also doesn’t need to have seen every possible obstacle. A rock in the road may be new. A collision is not. The system avoids the outcome, not the specific cause. The results are measurable. In an independent IIHS study, Waymo’s driverless vehicles were involved in 68% fewer crashes per mile than human drivers. IT operations still works the other way around. It starts from cause: detect, diagnose, then fix. The November 12 timeline shows exactly that. The first explanation was elevated load. Then it was corrected: servers were dropping out. The overwhelmed process was named hours later. Recovery took close to a day. That’s the equivalent of braking only after investigating why there’s traffic. When you can’t stop, move over safely There’s a second lesson in how the car behaves. When it can’t stop in its lane, it doesn’t just brake harder. It moves over, but only into a lane it knows is clear. Every large organization should have that, at a minimum: a safe diversion path for its critical business services. Not just redundancy on paper, but an alternate path that is known to be able to take the load. November 12 shows why the word safe matters. Microsoft had an alternate path. Teams failed over from an alternative gateway onto the primary one. But the path it moved onto was already carrying Exchange Online, running a months-old defect, with 14% of its capacity gone. The diversion didn’t avoid the collision. It moved into an occupied lane. This is one of the things I learned building historical intelligence. Safe diversion became one of its core actions, because the objectives were near-zero MTTR and no business disruption. History tells you which paths exist, how much load each one can actually absorb, and how each behaved the last time traffic shifted onto it. That’s what makes a diversion safe instead of just another move. Root cause should be a lookup, not an investigation About ten years ago, I worked on what we called incident avoidance. The approach was simple in principle. We started from the business: KPIs extracted from historical data, and past Severity-1 incidents, to identify which business impact areas mattered and which infrastructure contributed to them. We built the service dependency map first. Then we layered infrastructure metric streams on top, and watched every node on that map for anomalies using time series observation. When something deviated, we didn’t diagnose live. We pulled the root cause from possibilities that were already observed, because every node on the dependency map was already being watched. Root cause became a lookup: which upstream nodes are anomalous right now? We did this with classic machine learning. No LLMs, no foundation models, none of today’s tooling. Time series anomaly detection and dependency mapping were enough to protect the user experience. Apply that to November 12. With the dependency map in place, a load shift onto the gateway, a recent change on its connection path, and reduced headroom would have surfaced together as a known risk pattern. The safety-first actions could have been pre-decided: shed or reroute load, roll back the most recent change on that path, protect capacity. All of it before 80% of the gateway went dark. So why doesn’t this happen? This is the part that bewilders me. The company hit by this outage builds observability and application performance monitoring tools for its customers. It doesn’t lack data or tooling. Nobody does at that scale. It lacks intent. And intent follows ROI. Avoidance produces a non-event. Non-events don’t show up anywhere: Nobody gets credit for the outage that didn’t happen. Shipping speed is measured every sprint. Avoided risk never is. Service credits are small next to what customers lose , so even the cost of failure looks manageable from the inside. So detect-and-recover wins by default. It’s visible. It’s measurable. A thousand engineers on a bridge call looks like commitment. Avoidance looks like nothing at all. Meanwhile, managed services is projected at roughly $460 billion this year, growing past $700 billion by 2031. Most of that spend still buys people working tickets after something breaks, not intelligence that keeps it from breaking. Microsoft’s remediation list reflects the same pattern. Revert the code. Add capacity. Add monitoring for traffic redirection. Add guardrails on traffic distribution. All sensible, and all aimed at this specific failure. None of it changes how the next change gets evaluated against everything else happening at the same time. The missing investment: historical intelligence This is the point I keep coming back to, and the one I keep seeing missing. Enterprises invest in monitoring. They invest in observability dashboards, alerting and AIOps tools. What they don’t invest in is the foundation underneath: historical intelligence. Historical intelligence starts with discovery and dependency mapping: what exists, what talks to what, and which business services ride on which infrastructure. Then it attaches past behavior to that map, good and bad. How each component behaved under normal load and under peak. What every change on a path did before. Which combinations of change, load and capacity preceded past incidents, and which ones passed safely. With that foundation in place, three things change: Change approval gets informed. A change on the gateway’s connection path is evaluated against how similar changes behaved, at that capacity, under that load, before it’s approved. Anomalies get context. A load shift isn’t just a spike on a dashboard. It’s a known pattern on a known path with known consequences. Root cause is already there. The possibilities were observed before the incident, so nobody reconstructs the dependency map on a bridge call at midnight. Without it, every incident is investigated as if it were the first of its kind. With it, most of them are recognized before they start. Make the non-event visible The way out is the same one that made incident avoidance fundable in the first place: start from business outcomes, not infrastructure metrics. When avoidance is tied to revenue at risk and to the history of past Severity-1 incidents, the ROI becomes visible. “This pattern cost us this much last year, and here is how often it hasn’t recurred since.” That turns a non-event into a number a CFO can approve. The questions every CIO should be asking aren’t about tools: Have we invested in historical intelligence, with discovery and dependency mapping as its foundation, or only in monitoring? Which of our recent changes touch a critical path, and how do they behave under peak load at reduced capacity? Is our service dependency map built before the incident, or reconstructed during it? When a known risk pattern appears, is the safety-first action already decided? Does every critical business service have a safe diversion path, one we know can take the load? Do we measure the incidents we avoided, or only the ones we recovered from? Autonomous vehicles are proving every day that streaming signals, history and pre-decided action can avoid outcomes in a far messier world than a data center. The technology for IT operations has existed for a decade. What’s missing is the investment in historical intelligence that makes it work. It’s not legacy. It’s architecture. And it’s intent. This article is part of the Enterprise Intelligence series on building intelligence that drives peak business performance.

entries.title: Teaching AI to Unlearn: Why Elimination Starts With Questioning How We Work Today
entries.description: AI trained on history repeats history. To eliminate work, it first has to unlearn the assumption that the work is necessary.
entries.text: AI trained on history repeats history. To eliminate work, it first has to unlearn the assumption that the work is necessary. A frontier model was recently handed the raw weights of a small open-weight model that kept falling into repetitive reasoning loops. No training loop. No gradients. Fifty forward passes. It traced the habit to two layers, removed a single direction from 64 columns in each, and changed 0.016% of the weights. Math accuracy went from under 8% to over 48%. Most of the coverage went straight to AGI. That is not what caught my attention. What caught my attention is simpler: a habit inside a model can be located and removed. That matters to anyone building intelligence meant to do something other than repeat how work is done today. Before AI can eliminate work, it has to unlearn the assumption that the work is necessary. AI learns yesterday’s operating model Every model we put into enterprise operations learns from history: tickets, alerts, runbooks, resolutions. History is a record of how we worked, not how we should have worked. So the model gets very good at doing yesterday faster. Here is a simple example. Enterprises invested heavily in control planes: virtualization, converged, hyperconverged, cloud. Every one of them ships with built-in monitoring. Yet most organizations still layer open-source or commercial monitoring tools on top, because we were taught that operations needs monitoring tools. When we built historical intelligence on our platform, none of the dispositions it produced asked why the monitoring tool existed at all. The data never asked. No one in the data ever asked. The model learned the modality as a given. This is not a monitoring problem. Every domain has its version: approvals that a policy engine already enforces, reconciliations a system already guarantees, handoffs that exist only because two teams were organized that way years ago. A model trained on that history will automate all of it, beautifully. Labels teach instances, not principles So we taught it. We labeled event-driven alerts and tickets from a monitoring tool so the model would question why that tool existed. It worked, for that tool. The next time the pipeline ran, a different tool showed up. The model did not recognize the same pattern. We labeled again. The same happened with platforms. We kept building known machines and known behaviors, one at a time. What we had taught was “question Tool X.” What we needed was “question any layer that duplicates what the platform underneath already does.” We experimented with weights and temperature in the harness to get consistent dispositions. Temperature was never the real lever. It changes how randomly a model samples, not what it believes. The lever is the weights, or the activations flowing through them. That is why this research matters to me. Question the modality, keep the gap Unlearning does not mean rejecting. A crude version would eliminate every monitoring tool, including the ones that matter. Application performance monitoring is the clean example. Control planes see infrastructure: host health, capacity, VM state. They do not see code-level traces, transaction flows across services, or what the end user actually experiences. APM covers a real gap. It survives the question. So the target is not “monitoring tools are unnecessary.” The target is the shortcut: assuming the tool is needed without asking. For every layer, the model should ask three things. What does the native layer already cover? What does this add? Is the remainder worth paying for? That gives three outcomes, not two: Eliminate when the overlap is complete. Keep when the tool covers a real gap. Shrink when it does both: keep the tool, drop the overlapping modules and licenses. Put the disposition in the model, keep the facts in retrieval The coverage line keeps moving. Cloud platforms now ship native tracing and application insights. Part of what justified APM five years ago may be redundant today. If you train “APM is required” into the weights, you have just created the next status quo to unlearn. So the architecture splits: The disposition to question lives in the model. Teach it with contrasting reasoning: one trace that accepts the modality, one that questions it. On open-weight models, that difference can steer the model at inference or train a small adapter. Use synthetic scenarios across domains so it learns the pattern, not the products: monitoring over native telemetry, ticketing over self-healing platforms, approvals over policy engines. The facts live in retrieval. A capability map of what each platform natively does, refreshed as platforms change. New tools map to capabilities, not labels. A tool the model has never seen gets classified by what it does and compared against native coverage. No relabeling. Only the capability map changes, and that is data, not training. This is where the weight-space research earns its place. If “skip the question” is a localized habit, like the looping in that study, it can be found with a small set of contrasting examples and suppressed. And you can check inside the model that it is gone, instead of hoping your tests catch every case. What this doesn’t solve It removes habits, not beliefs. The looping fix worked because the behavior was concentrated in a few places. A belief spread across a model’s world knowledge is much harder to remove. It only unlocks what is already there. The same procedure on a smaller model produced no gain, because that model never had the capability. The model must already be able to reason “this layer is redundant.” It is early. The study is unreviewed, used one frontier model, and worked on small targets. Someone still has to define what questioning looks like. That is the leadership job. These tools make unlearning cheaper, more targeted and verifiable. They do not decide which modality deserves to be questioned. The industry is focused on teaching AI to do today’s work faster. The harder and more valuable problem is teaching it to stop accepting today’s work as a given. If your AI learned everything it knows from how your organization worked yesterday, who is teaching it to question yesterday? This article is part of the Enterprise Intelligence series on building intelligence that drives peak business performance.

entries.title: The Restart That Shouldn’t Have Happened
entries.description: Decision models don't explain their answers. In enterprise operations, the fix isn't better prompts. It's training the why, verifying state before deciding, and a harness that lets humans see what a decision rested on.
entries.text: Fast decision models need trained intent and verified context, not just assembled context. Decision models are having a moment. Jev, Cloudflare’s Clef and OpenAI’s Decisions API skip the verbose reasoning and return structured JSON with a confidence score. Developers love the speed and the determinism. In a recent VentureBeat piece , Dattaraj Rao of Persistent Systems named the catch. These models don’t explain themselves. If the model won’t reason for you, he argues, you have to reason for it upfront, through context design. Context matters. But we lived this problem on our AI-native operations platform, and my experience says context is not enough. A model never trained on why a disposition applies won’t reach it, however good the context. And no model, fast or verbose, can be relied on to tell you what it was actually thinking. The ticket An incident came in: a cloud VM on Azure was unavailable. We asked our disposition model what to do. It returned automate: restart the VM . Then we asked the obvious question. Why? What were you thinking? There was no answer. A classification has no reasoning to recover. What the right answer was The first step should never have been a restart. It should have been a check. Is the VM actually down? Check the Azure control plane. If it’s up, why is it unreachable? Check the network path. In this case the VM was running. The VPN was down. The “VM unavailable” ticket was a last-mile network symptom, not a compute failure. A restart would have done nothing except add risk to a healthy machine. The correct disposition was eliminate . Why the model said restart The model learned from history, and history lied to it. In most ticket data, “VM unreachable, restarted, resolved” looks like a success story. Often the restart had nothing to do with it. The network recovered on its own, or the ticket auto-closed. The label recorded the action, not the cause. So the model learned a symptom-to-action correlation. Better context design on the ticket text alone would not have fixed that. The ticket simply did not contain the truth. Three layers, not one Rao frames context as the fix. In my experience it is one of three layers, and the least sufficient on its own. Train on the why. Label historical dispositions with verified cause and the reasoning for eliminate vs automate vs human assist. Without this, eliminate is unreachable. Context given to a model that never learned the why is like teaching a parrot a new word: it repeats, it doesn’t understand. Verify before deciding. Run deterministic checks first: control-plane status, network path (VPN, gateway, security rules). “VM running + VPN down” then cannot map to “restart.” Make the why checkable. Train the model to produce its rationale before the disposition, anchored to verified evidence. If rationale and evidence disagree, the decision does not execute. Don’t ask the model what it was thinking Even then, the model can’t truly explain itself. A pure decision model has no reasoning to report. A generative model asked “why” afterward writes a plausible reconstruction, not a readout of what drove the output. Research on chain-of-thought faithfulness has shown stated reasoning often leaves out the real cause. So responsibility for the why sits with human assist, and the harness must give humans something to reason with: Confidence: calibrated, with a threshold that routes to a human Evidence state: what was verified and what wasn’t Precedents: the historical tickets the decision most resembles. Here it would have exposed the contaminated “restart, resolved” history Conflicts: disposition vs evidence, such as restart while the VM shows running Confidence alone would not have caught our case. The restart was likely a confident call. The model decides. The harness exposes. The human deduces and corrects. Each correction becomes training on the why. From one ticket to an elimination program “Eliminate” is rarely a single-ticket decision. It comes from historical intelligence: seeing that a class of VM-down alerts is really a recurring network cause. That pattern becomes a transformation program: 1. Remove the alert that generates the misleading ticket. 2. Reconfigure detection to check the cloud control plane and the network path together. 3. Re-point the action to what actually fixes it: recreate or restore the VPN, not restart the VM. 4. Re-label history with verified root cause, so the next model doesn’t learn the same wrong lesson. The ticket disappears. Not because we automated it faster, but because it should never have existed. The takeaway Decision models make explainability the builder’s job. In enterprise operations, that job is not prompt engineering. It is training the why, verifying state before anything decides, and building a harness that shows humans what a decision rested on. Speed without verified context just gets you to the wrong restart faster. Sources VentureBeat, Decision models like Jev don’t explain their answers. That makes context your problem (November 7, 2026) This article is part of the Enterprise Intelligence series on building organization-specific intelligence that drives peak business performance.

entries.title: The Context to Eliminate
entries.description: Snowflake's Business Ontology gives a data platform the top-down context to eliminate work, not just automate it. Why the platforms won't lead with elimination, and what enterprises should do instead.
entries.text: Snowflake now has the context to tell enterprises what work should not exist. Its latest announcement uses that context to automate the work instead. At Expedition 2026, Snowflake announced three things: a Business Ontology framework, expanded agent governance through Cortex AI Gateway, and autonomous data engineering, where agents build, monitor and troubleshoot data pipelines with less human intervention. The pattern is familiar. Salesforce has its AI Control Plane, ServiceNow has AI Control Tower, and SAP has governed Joule agents. Every platform is racing to become the place where agents run and are controlled. None of them is asking which work the agents should be doing in the first place. The automation reflex Faster troubleshooting still assumes the failure. An agent that repairs a broken pipeline faster accepts that the pipeline will break. It makes failure cheaper to handle. It does not ask why the failure keeps happening. I have watched this reflex play out in every wave of IT operations, from runbook automation and scripting to AIOps. The ticket gets resolved faster, the incident closes sooner, and the work that caused both stays exactly where it was. Agents make the reflex more powerful, not less. Governing agents like employees preserves the work. Snowflake describes giving agents the kind of oversight applied to employees: access rules, monitoring, cost controls, audit trails. That is sensible. But it treats agents as digital labor slotted into today’s operating model. It governs the work. It does not question it. Context from the top, telemetry from below Business Ontology is the most important part of the announcement. It lets an organization set approved definitions for its business concepts, so two agents don’t give incompatible answers from the same accurate data. That is top-down context: what revenue, a customer or a claim actually means in this business. The platform already holds the bottom-up half. Snowflake sees every pipeline run and failure, the lineage from source to report, and which tables and metrics are queried, by whom and how often. Put those together and you have what elimination needs. When I built an AI-native operations platform, the hardest part was assembling exactly this: business context on one side, operational history on the other, joined well enough to say which work serves the business and which doesn’t. We called it historical intelligence, and it decided what to eliminate before anything was automated. Snowflake has both halves in one place. The questions that context can answer With ontology and telemetry joined, a data platform could answer elimination questions instead of only automation ones: Which pipelines, tables or metrics map to no approved business concept, or have no consumer? Retire them. Every one an agent maintains is cost with no outcome. Which recurring failures trace back to the same upstream source or contract? Fix the cause once, rather than having an agent troubleshoot the symptom forever. Which near-duplicate metrics exist only because definitions diverged? Once the ontology settles the definition, collapse them. Only what survives those questions should be automated. Only what can’t be automated should go to a human. That order is the difference between an agent-run estate and a smaller, better one. Why the platforms won’t lead with it Consumption pricing rewards more work. It pays for more compute, more pipelines and more agent activity. Elimination cuts all three. A vendor billed on usage has little reason to tell you a third of your usage shouldn’t exist. Ontology is not purpose. It defines what a term means, not which business outcome that term should move. A clean definition of “claim” says nothing about whether claims take too long to settle, or whether the data flowing around them shortens that time. Elimination needs that last link from data to outcome. Without it, you can tidy definitions and still keep running work that doesn’t matter. What enterprises should do Don’t wait for the platform to ask the question. Before you switch on agents that build and repair pipelines: 1. Build historical intelligence first. Use run history, failure history and consumption data to find what is unused, duplicated or failing for the same reason again and again. 2. Eliminate before you automate. Retire what serves no outcome, fix recurring causes at the source, and only then hand the remainder to agents, with humans assisting where judgment is needed. 3. Tie the work to business KPIs, and buy it that way. Ask vendors what outcome they guarantee, not how much activity they will run. Outcome-based terms are the only ones that reward elimination. Snowflake has built the context layer the industry needed. The question is whether it gets used to run more work faster, or to run less work that matters more. The platforms will default to the first. Enterprises should insist on the second. Sources SiliconANGLE, Snowflake expands agentic AI platform with business context and governance tools (November 3, 2026) This article is part of the Enterprise Intelligence series on building intelligence that drives peak business performance.

entries.title: The PR That Ships Without Comments
entries.description: The LLM's power is reasoning to a decision, not faster code. The metric that matters is a PR that ships with no review comments, and it starts with setting the objective.
entries.text: Proton’s CTO, Bart Butler, recently told his engineers their job has fundamentally changed. Writing code is no longer the job. In his words, the job is now to help the LLM “write better code faster.” ( Business Insider ) He is right about the first half. The engineer is now a lead of models and agents, not a typist. But look at the measure. Better code, faster. That is still a throughput metric. If the goal is more code in less time, we have taken the LLM’s biggest weakness, the wall of text, and pointed it at our codebase. The business never asked for faster code. It asked for a claim settled sooner, a higher yield, an order delivered on time. Code is only the path to that. Two prompts, two outcomes Compare two requests to the same model. The first: generate this service so it runs in Java. The second: generate this service following our design principles and architecture, against our data model, consuming the services we already expose, and passing the tests written for this requirement. Both produce code that compiles. Only the second has a real chance of passing review without a single comment. That is the metric that matters. A pull request that goes through with no feedback goes to production sooner. It is what sets time to release, and time to release is what meets the business objective. Lines of code per hour do not. I’m not alone in seeing this. Sergey Marchuk, CTO at Oxagile, wrote in Forbes this week that agents have made code cheaper to produce while making ambiguity more expensive. He cites Harvard researchers who found that coding agents increased lines of code by 30%, while the time from pull request to merge rose 49%. More code went in, and it took longer to get out. His answer is more structure around the agent: a specification checked for gaps before implementation, a context harness kept in the repository, and named human sign-off at each stage. That is the right instinct. But the gap check rests on the spec and on whoever reviews it. In my experience, the gaps that hurt most are the ones nobody thought to write down. When the requirements pipeline carries the organization’s own history (which requirements went missing, which tests were never written, which defects kept coming back), the LLM can flag that white space while the objective is still being defined. The model is ready. The context isn’t. Today’s LLMs, and the harness around them, can already do the second prompt well. Capability is not the constraint. The constraint is knowledge. To write that second prompt, the developer or lead has to know the design principles, the architecture, the data model, every exposed service, and the test intent behind the requirement. Few people hold all of that in their head. Fewer can feed it to a model on every request. So the model reasons over whatever thin context it is given, and fills the gaps with plausible code. Reviewers catch the gaps. The PR goes back. Release slips. The business objective waits. What we learned: start with the objective, not the data We faced this directly when we built SDLC intelligence for a manufacturer and an insurer. We did not start by collecting data. We started by defining the objective: produce a service whose PR gets no review feedback, goes through to production, and moves a business outcome such as claim processing time, yield, or order processing, in its own context. Only then did we gather data sources, and we did it structurally: 1. Requirements, user stories and epics 2. Test cases 3. Code and data repositories 4. Published APIs and services 5. Historical defects The step that made it work came next. We gave the model the objective and the sources, and asked it a different question: is this enough to meet the objective, and where is the white space? The model came back with gaps. A requirement with no test. A data assumption no one had written down. A localization and currency rule that had never been captured in requirements, and had shown up only as defects. We closed each gap and ran the loop again. Objective, sources, white space, close, repeat. That loop engineering is what turned “build this service” into an outcome-based, measurable request. The results were fewer requirement gaps, better code quality, bugs eliminated rather than fixed, and shorter time to release. Objectives build better engineers, and better leaders This way of working builds better engineers. You cannot set an objective like “no review comments and a faster claim” without understanding the business context and the value at stake. The coder becomes a developer who knows why the service exists. The same holds well beyond code. A business leader who understands the outcome and its impact can set clear objectives for an agent and run the loop until the output aligns. Leadership stops spending time correcting work that was aimed at the wrong target. A simple example I heard recently: an order-to-shipment report versus an order-to-delivery report. Shipment tells you the warehouse did its part. Delivery tells you whether the customer got what they ordered, when promised. The second is the status that means something to the business. But if the objective is not set that way, the agent will not know. It will build the first report, accurately and quickly, and it will still be the wrong answer. The engineer’s real job So yes, the engineer’s job has changed. But it is not to help the LLM write code faster. It is to define the outcome, assemble the context, and close the white space the model surfaces. The model’s power is in reasoning over that context to a decision: is this enough, what is missing, what should be built. Generating the code is the easy part. This is the same point I made in The Missing Objective : a model is only as useful as the objective we train and point it at. Point it at faster code and you get more code. Point it at a PR that ships without comments and a business outcome that moves, and you get release velocity that actually matters. Sources Business Insider, Proton CTO’s AI manifesto for software engineers (October 2026) Sergey Marchuk, Forbes Technology Council, “The Engineering Behind an AI-Native Software Development Life Cycle” (November 2, 2026) Part of the Enterprise Intelligence series.

entries.title: Automate or Augment? Both Skip the First Question
entries.description: Every major AI-and-jobs study asks whether AI will automate or augment work. None asks whether the work should exist at all. Digital banks show what elimination looks like — and how incumbents can get there with historical and market intelligence.
entries.text: Every major study of AI and work asks some version of one question: will AI automate this task, or augment the person doing it? The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 asks it. Anthropic’s Economic Index, which measures how AI is actually being used, asks it. On stage in Davos this January, technology CEOs answered it the same way: AI augments people, it doesn’t replace them. None of them asks the question that comes first: should this work exist at all? On Thursday, I argued that elimination is the missing objective in how we train and deploy AI. This piece looks at the same gap from the other side: how we measure AI’s impact on work. What the declining-jobs list really shows WEF’s 2025 list of the fastest-declining roles reads like this: postal service clerks, bank tellers, data entry clerks, cashiers, accounting and payroll clerks, stock-keeping clerks. The report credits automation, digital payments and self-service. Look at that list as a process architect instead of a labor economist, and it isn’t a list of jobs being automated. It’s a list of workflows that exist because of how information used to move. Data entry exists because data was captured in one place and needed in another. Reconciliation exists because two systems disagree. Teller transactions exist because the customer had to come to the money. Automate those workflows and you get a faster version of an unnecessary process. Augment them and you get a smarter person running an unnecessary process. Neither changes what the business delivers to its customer. The bank that never built the workflow Digital banks didn’t automate tellers. They designed a bank without branches, so the teller workflow never existed. Onboarding, identity checks, credit decisions and servicing were built as one digital flow instead of a chain of handoffs. That shows up where it matters: for the customer. As of October 1, 2026, Bankrate puts the national average savings yield at 0.65% APY, while the best high-yield accounts, mostly at online banks, pay around 4%. Lower overhead is the reason usually given. To be fair, not all of that gap is efficiency. Some of it is customer-acquisition spending, and some of it is that incumbents can pay less because their deposits are sticky. But efficiency is what makes the higher rate sustainable rather than promotional. That is elimination expressed as a customer outcome: a structural advantage passed straight to the customer. That is what peak business performance should look like. Why the research can’t see elimination Task-level frameworks inherit today’s org chart. They start from existing occupations and their task lists, then score each task. A task that should disappear doesn’t get a score of its own. It just gets labeled “automatable.” Usage data has the same blind spot. Anthropic’s January 2026 index found augmentation narrowly ahead of automation on Claude.ai, roughly 52% to 45%. On the business API side, the picture flips: about three-quarters of interactions were automation, which Anthropic reads as businesses automating routine back-office workflows like email, document processing and scheduling. Nobody is measuring whether those workflows should exist. Both categories describe AI doing existing work or helping someone do it. There is no category for “redesigned so this step is gone.” That gap isn’t academic. If the measurement has no column for elimination, the transformation roadmap won’t have one either. How incumbents get there: historical plus market intelligence A digital bank eliminated work by design, on a greenfield. An incumbent has to do it inside a running operation. That takes two kinds of intelligence. Historical intelligence tells you what can go. Years of tickets, cases, transactions and logs show which workflows are failure demand, rework, or workarounds for gaps between systems. Each one gets a disposition: eliminate it, hand it to agentic AI, or keep a human in the loop with assistance. The order matters. Eliminate first, automate what can’t be eliminated, and assist humans on the rest. On the AI-native shared services platform I led R&D for, that order is what produced 60–80% work elimination. Market intelligence tells you what has to go. When the business asks for “faster and cheaper,” it usually means a competitor is already there. Benchmarks like onboarding time, claims speed and order-to-delivery tell you which gap is real and how large it is. A savings rate six times the national average is a market-intelligence signal. It tells an incumbent bank exactly how much structural cost a competitor has already removed. IT shouldn’t wait for the business to raise that gap. With both kinds of intelligence in hand, it can surface the gap first. The people question WEF’s real concern is the workforce, and it’s a fair one. Elimination is not a headcount plan. Eliminate the work, redeploy the people. Move them to the work the eliminated process was crowding out: customer relationships, exception judgment, new products. That is why elimination has to be led by change management, not by tooling. It means changing the operating model, then transforming and transitioning. It’s also why enterprises need an elimination office: someone has to own the question before anyone buys the automation. Three questions before “automate or augment” 1. Why does this workflow exist, and what failure or gap created it? 2. Who already runs without it: a competitor, a digital native, another business unit? 3. If we removed it, what would the customer get from the difference? Answer those first. Then decide what’s left to automate. Sources World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025 (January 2025); declining roles as summarised by Gulf News Anthropic, Anthropic Economic Index Report: Economic Primitives (January 2026) Free Press Journal, “WEF 2026: AI Won’t Replace Human Jobs But Will Augment Employees At Scale” (January 2026) Bankrate, national average savings account rate survey (October 1, 2026) World Economic Forum, Jobs of Tomorrow: Large Language Models and Jobs (September 2023) This article is part of my ongoing series on elimination-led enterprise intelligence: building intelligence that drives peak business performance by eliminating work first. entries.title: The Missing Objective: Why AI Keeps Automating Work That Shouldn’t Exist
entries.description: Every LLM leap came from changing what we train models to do. One objective is still missing: elimination. Why enterprises need an elimination office.
entries.text: Every language model rests on one foundation: predicting the next word. To do that well, it learns the patterns behind language, and from those patterns comes its ability to reason and decide. What we point that ability at is up to us. Most of the industry points it at completing tasks. I have pointed the same capability at a different order: eliminate first, automate what cannot be eliminated, then seek human assist. A HackerNoon piece by Vasudev Gupta traces the evolution of LLMs through exactly this lens: what we train them to do. First predict the next token, then be a helpful assistant, then reason before answering, and now act until the job is done. Each leap came from changing the objective, and the deliverable has moved from an answer to finished work. It is an accurate account. But one objective is absent from it, and from almost every enterprise AI roadmap I see: elimination. The objective nobody trains for An agent rewarded for finishing the task will finish the task. It will never conclude that the task should not exist. Reaching that conclusion takes a different objective: extract the pattern behind recurring work, trace it to its cause, and remove the cause. Without that objective, the generative AI evolution leads to one place: task automation. We get faster, cheaper execution of the operating model we already have, including all the work that never needed doing. Four cases: the answer was there, but only when asked why I have put real operational scenarios to models, both frontier and open weight. The pattern is consistent. The deletion ticket. A user at a manufacturing company raised a ticket to delete a line item they were not allowed to delete. The RPA-era answer was to automate the deletion. BPOs still sell that service, and agentic AI companies now convert those bots into agents, sold as a service or as the agent itself. Nobody asks the real question: is the permission model right? If the user should be able to delete it, fix the role. If not, the ticket should never be raised. The no-action monitoring ticket. An alert created a ticket assigned to a human, who simply waited until it auto-closed. The model’s disposition was to automate, since no human was needed. When I asked why it was a ticket at all, it agreed: configure the wait in the monitoring tool and delete the alert. The disk space batch failure. A full disk kept breaking a batch process. The model produced a script to check space, clean up and rerun. When I pointed out that an earlier batch step creates a huge file that is never moved, it agreed the fix belonged inside the batch process itself. The campus Wi-Fi. A large campus area network had engineers stationed on site, running to every Wi-Fi issue. The model proposed automating the ticket at the controller level, so each ticket would trigger a reset. The elimination disposition is different: configure the wireless controller to detect a failing access point and restart it when it is safe to do so. That check-and-act capability already exists in the controller. When I pointed this out, the model agreed. In every case the model could reach the elimination answer. It only got there because a human asked why. The capability is present. The default is not. The hidden cost of automating symptoms Look at what each default answer produces: a bot, a script, an agent. Each is a new artifact that someone must own, monitor, patch and eventually migrate. Each elimination answer produces nothing new. It rewires a platform the enterprise already pays for: a role permission, an alert setting, a batch step, a controller capability. This repeats across every layer: business process, application, data and infrastructure. Work was first set up for humans, then scripted, and is now being converted into agents. Each wave carries the previous wave’s unexamined work forward and adds its own maintenance cost. Few organizations count that cost, because it is spread across teams and budgets. Why this is a training problem Models default to automation for reasons built into how they are trained: Pretraining data. Decades of RPA, BPO and agent-vendor material make “automate the ticket” the dominant pattern in the corpus. Human feedback. RLHF rewards answering the request as framed. The ticket says fix it, so fixing it is rated helpful. Questioning whether the ticket should exist can read as unresponsive. Agentic reinforcement learning. Agents are rewarded for completing tasks. A closed ticket is a cheap, verifiable reward. A ticket that never recurs plays out over months and across systems, so nobody trains on it. The HackerNoon article makes the point that progress comes from designing data that teaches the right objective. Elimination needs exactly that data: Preference pairs where rewiring the existing platform ranks above automating the symptom. Rubrics that reward asking why the work exists, checking native platform capability first, and avoiding new artifacts to maintain. Outcome rewards drawn from historical operational data: did the pattern stop recurring? Enterprises already hold this data in their tickets, logs and process history. Very few use it this way. Why no enterprise has an elimination office If elimination is the better objective, why does nobody fund it? Because almost no one in the decision chain is paid for work that disappears. Service providers. BPOs bill per FTE or ticket, agent vendors per agent or consumption, integrators per build. Elimination shrinks every one of those revenue lines. Platform vendors. Pointing customers to capability they already own generates no upsell, so account teams pitch new AI add-ons instead. Budgets. Boards ask for an AI strategy, so funding flows to visible agent programs. A ticket that never happened cannot be demoed. Silos. The four cases above span access, monitoring, batch and network teams. Each automates within its lane. Nobody owns a cause that cuts across them. Metrics. Managers are often measured on team size, and providers on SLAs and ticket volume. Elimination makes both look smaller. Perceived risk. Rewiring a production platform feels invasive. An agent on top feels safe and reversible, even though it costs more to run over time. There is a precedent. ITIL problem management has existed for decades and is essentially elimination, yet it remains one of the least funded practices in IT. Lean made eliminating waste central to manufacturing, but that discipline never carried over into IT operations. The case for an elimination office LLMs, MCP servers and agents will not deliver their full value until someone asks whether the work should exist. That question needs an owner. An elimination office would: Own the “should this exist?” decision before any automation is funded: eliminate first, automate what cannot be eliminated, then human assist. Work from historical intelligence across tickets, logs and process data, not workshops and opinions. Be measured on demand removed and business outcomes moved, not tasks automated. Report to the CFO or COO , who own cost and performance outcomes, with change management built in so elimination reads as removing waste, not headcount. Pair with outcome-based commercial models , so providers are paid for results rather than activity. The HackerNoon article closes by asking what we reward agents for. My answer: reward them for work that never has to happen. The model already knows the answer. It just was not trained to ask. Part of an ongoing series on enterprise intelligence: building intelligence into every process, application, data layer and infrastructure so it drives peak business performance. entries.title: Good Is Not Good Enough: The Intelligence Hiding in Your Own Data
entries.description: Fintech turned business processes into technology services. The next, bigger conversion turns business judgment into intelligence, and most enterprises already hold the playbook in their own historical data.
entries.text: The next competitive divide will not come from who buys the best model. It will come from who converts their own business judgment into intelligence. The last great conversion We have seen a version of this before. Financial services firms became fintech firms when they learned to turn a business process into a technology service. Payments, lending and onboarding stopped being back-office procedures and became products. Intelligence is a far more powerful conversion. Fintech codified the process. Intelligence codifies the judgment inside the process: which claim to fast-track, which batch will miss yield, where order-to-invoice is quietly leaking. A codified process stays roughly the same once built. Codified judgment compounds, because every decision and outcome makes it sharper. Same platforms, different winners Most business domains already run on a small set of common platforms. Wealth management onboards clients on shared wealth platforms. P&C insurers run claims and policy on Guidewire. Retailers run on Manhattan and similar suites. Manufacturers run on PLM, SCADA and Oracle order management. The processes are common too: onboarding, claims, policy administration, order-to-cash, production scheduling. Development teams reuse the same open-source components across all of them. Yet the outcomes are wildly uneven. Facebook figured out social networking better than MySpace. Fuji navigated the shift Kodak missed. Same era, same technology, different results. The platform was never the differentiator. How an enterprise runs its processes on that platform is. That difference is visible in the data, if anyone looks. Master intelligence When we built an AI-native operations platform, historical intelligence surfaced something we had not set out to find. Across enterprises on the same platforms, some had already reached a far higher level of efficiency. They got there through changes in process and configuration, not by buying different technology. That best-observed efficiency became a master intelligence for the domain. It worked as a loop: 1. Learn the benchmark. Historical data (tickets, logs, workflows and more) reveals the most efficient way a process actually runs on a given platform. 2. Evaluate new data against it. Each new set of operational data is compared with the master intelligence to find the gap. 3. Generate actionable intelligence. The gap becomes a concrete recommendation: eliminate the work, hand it to an agent, or assist a human. 4. Learn from human feedback. People explain when a recommendation is not practical for their enterprise, and the intelligence absorbs that context. This held across every layer we worked in: business process, application, data and infrastructure. The same approach drove 60–80% work elimination and 35%+ cost takeout in production. Two examples from the field The order that couldn’t ship. At several manufacturers on Oracle order management, users were not permitted to delete order line items. Every deletion needed an IT ticket, and those tickets sometimes took two to three days. Meanwhile, orders sat unready for shipment. Historical intelligence spotted the same pattern across companies. It also found one enterprise that had solved it with a change to how the underlying Oracle platform was configured. Applying that pattern eliminated the ticket entirely. Resolution time dropped to zero and orders were ready to ship immediately. This was a business process problem and an application problem at once, and no amount of faster ticket handling would have fixed it. The slow data build. In another case, the intelligence quickly traced a sluggish data build to how batch jobs were scheduled and the fact that they were not monitored. Nobody had connected the two. Fixing the schedule and adding monitoring removed the slowness at its source. We saw many more like these in the infrastructure layer. The pattern was the same each time: the fix already existed somewhere, hidden in the data. Your own history already holds it You do not need a cross-industry dataset to start. Every enterprise has its own “good is not good enough” cases buried in its historical data. They show up as recurring tickets that should never exist, as manual approvals that add days without adding control, and as workarounds teams have normalized. They also show up as the best-performing plant, region or team, whose way of working never spread to the rest. That internal best is your first master intelligence. Measure everything else against it, and the gap becomes your roadmap. Market intelligence: answer “faster and cheaper” before it’s asked In almost every engagement, the business eventually came back with the same request: can you do this faster and cheaper? When we looked closer, that request was rarely arbitrary. It usually meant a competitor had already achieved it. So we started building market intelligence for each domain alongside the historical intelligence. It turned out to be one of the most practical data points we could offer. We could show a wealth management firm that a competitor was onboarding assets in half the time, a P&C insurer that rivals were settling claims faster, and a manufacturer that peers had much shorter order-to-delivery times. That changes IT’s posture from reactive to proactive. Instead of waiting for the business to turn a competitive gap into a complaint or a requirement, intelligence can surface the gap first, show the efficiency level that is already possible, and arrive with the path to close it. In an age when everyone is talking about super intelligence, this is the minimum standard: know where you stand before the market tells you. The benchmarks have to be credible. Draw them from public disclosures, industry studies, customer-facing service levels and aggregated, anonymized operational data, never from any single company’s confidential records. Why boards aren’t driving it yet Few boards or CXOs are treating intelligence as a business asset to build. Four framing problems keep it small: Wrong owner. AI sits with the CIO as a tooling program, not with the P&L leader as a business capability. Wrong metric. Success is counted in copilot seats and hours saved, not in combined ratio, yield, DSO or revenue leakage. Wrong starting point. Companies pick a model first and hunt for use cases later, instead of mining their own decisions to find where intelligence pays. No product mindset. Nobody owns intelligence as a living asset that is versioned, measured and improved. Where to start 1. Pick one KPI that matters to the board. Claims cycle time, yield, order-to-cash leakage or DSO. Make the P&L leader the owner. 2. Build historical intelligence first. Mine tickets, logs, workflow and transaction data to establish your internal best and the gap to it. 3. Benchmark against the market. Know where competitors already are on that KPI before the business asks why you aren’t. 4. Eliminate before you automate. Remove work that should not exist, hand repeatable decisions to agents, and assist humans on the rest. 5. Lead with change management. Actionable intelligence only pays when the operating model changes with it: transform, then transition. 6. Treat the intelligence as a product. Version it, measure it against the KPI, and feed human feedback back into it. The moat is not the model Models are becoming commodities. Open-weight or frontier, they are increasingly interchangeable engines. What no competitor can download is the intelligence built from your own decisions and outcomes. Every company became a software company. The next winners will become intelligence companies, but only the ones that own and build on their decision data. The platforms are the same for everyone. The question is who starts building first. This article is part of my Enterprise Intelligence series on building intelligence into every business process, application, data and infrastructure layer to drive peak business performance.
